activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: When a plant's central vacuoles are full of water they press outward against the cell walls, and when they lose water the plant wilts.
story:
Maya pressed her nose against the glass of the tank where a green tree frog sat pretending to be a leaf. She was at the veterinary clinic waiting for her mother, who worked at the front desk, and she had her science homework spread across two chairs. The assignment asked her to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have, and she had gotten as far as "cell wall" before stalling.

"That looks like the poster my uncle made," said Leanna, who had come in with her cat's carrier and now leaned over Maya's paper. In the carrier, her cat, Mr. Biscuits, yowled in protest. Leanna pointed at a wilted pothos plant drooping on the windowsill beside them. "That plant's gone floppy. Your paper should say why."

Maya stared at the plant. It had been standing upright a week ago; she remembered admiring its glossy leaves while waiting for her mother. Something inside it had changed, but she could not see inside it, not without a microscope, and the clinic did not keep one for plants. "The cells lost something," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Like a balloon going soft."

Mr. Horváth, the veterinarian, came out to weigh Mr. Biscuits and overheard them. "There's a microscope in the back room," he said, "and a slice of onion skin in the fridge from a demo I do for school tours. Come see." Maya and Leanna took turns at the eyepiece while the cat growled. The onion cells looked like neat brick boxes, and inside each one Maya spotted a pale, rounded shape that shifted when she tapped the slide. "That's a vacuole," she said, remembering the diagram. "It stores water. Animal cells have little ones, but only plant cells have the big central kind." She looked back at the droopy pothos. "So those vacuoles must be empty-ish now. When they're full, they press outward against the cell walls and hold the plant up. When they lose water, the plant wilts." She grabbed the watering can by the sink.

"The wilt's only temporary," Leanna said. "My uncle's poster says that too, right before he tries to justify buying another houseplant he'll forget about."

On the wall near the window hung a bright flyer claiming vitamin water would cure any pet's lethargy. "That's propaganda," Maya said, wrinkling her nose. "It's just water."

That evening Maya wrote a note to leave on the clinic fridge for her mother: "Watered the pothos at 4:15. If it stands up by morning, my homework is right. P.S. I finished my diagram: cell walls, chloroplasts, and the big central vacuole are plant-only. Animal cells just have the membrane. Wish me luck."

The next afternoon Maya burst through the clinic door and ran to the windowsill. Every pothos leaf stood out firm and glossy, like a small green parade. "It worked," she whispered, and did a quiet fist pump beside the frog tank. Mr. Horváth walked by with a chart in his hand and gave her a thumbs up. "Vacuoles for the win," he said.

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: NIST's guidance says systems should not force people to change passwords on a schedule, only when there is evidence a password has been stolen.
story:
Carter sat on Cyrus's basement floor with a laptop open and a granola bar in his hand, trying to think of a password for the new game the whole class was playing. Cyrus had already typed his in, and it had taken him two seconds.

"Just use the same one you use for everything," Cyrus said, scrolling through the character menu. "Mine is my dog's name and my birthday. Easy."

"That's like locking every door in the neighborhood with the same key," Carter said. "Somebody gets one, they get the whole street." He bit off a chunk of granola bar and winced when a piece wedged between his teeth. "I want something better."

Ananya came down the stairs carrying her backpack. "My mom's office makes everyone pick a new password every single month. She keeps a sticky note on her monitor with the current one."

"That's worse," Carter said slowly, the way he talked when an idea was still assembling itself. "If you have to change it all the time, you run out of good ideas, so you end up with password1, password2, password3." He pulled out his phone. "Let me look something up."

He found a government standards page, and read parts of it out loud. "NIST's guidance says systems should not force people to change passwords on a schedule, only when there is evidence a password has been stolen."

"Who's NIST?" Cyrus asked.

"The National Institute of Standards and Technology. They basically write the rulebook." Carter set the phone down. "So the monthly thing at your mom's office is actually against the guidance. It's obsolete, like a rule somebody wrote in the nineties and never updated."

Ananya dropped onto the couch. "I'm telling my mom. She'll be thrilled."

"First, watch this." Carter turned back to the laptop and typed a long password, four random words strung together. He tried a few login attempts with wrong guesses, then the right one. "See? I don't need to change it every month. I just need it long and weird, and I check if somebody's seen it." He pointed at the ceiling. "There's a motion sensor up there, right? You guard the door that way, not by moving the door once a month."

Cyrus looked at his dog's name typed into six different accounts and groaned. "Okay, fine. Give me four words."

"Rhino taco battery kazoo," Carter said.

Cyrus typed it in, then paused. "If I tell you, isn't that the same key again?"

Carter handed him the granola bar. "You're learning. Pick your own rhino."

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: Every extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords: using only lowercase letters, adding one more letter makes 26 times as many possibilities to guess.
story:
Peyton slid into her seat in the computer lab just as the login screen appeared, and beside her Maika was already typing. "Six letters, all lowercase," Maika said. "Banana. Well, not banana, but six letters. Long enough, right?" Peyton leaned over. Something about that bothered her, the way a loose thread bothers you before you can see where it leads. Six letters felt short, but she couldn't say why, and she wanted to know why.

She grabbed a scratch paper. "Let me try something." She started with one letter. With only lowercase letters, one spot had 26 choices. Two spots would be 26 times 26. She wrote it out: 26, then 676, then 17,576, and kept multiplying until her hand hurt. At six letters the number stretched past three hundred million. "Okay, that sounds big," she admitted. Maika smirked and reached for the mouse.

"Wait," Peyton said. "Watch." She did seven letters next, and the number jumped to over eight billion. She underlined it twice. "Every extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords. Adding one more letter makes 26 times as many possibilities to guess." Seven letters wasn't just a little bigger than six, it was twenty-six times bigger, like a stairway where every step was a whole new staircase. "So your six letters? A computer could chew through all of them way faster than something twice as long."

Ms. Wong walked by and paused at their monitor. "What have we classified this as, correct or risky?" "Risky," Peyton said. "Also, Maika uses the same one everywhere. Isn't that like one key for your house, your locker, and your bike lock?" Maika frowned. "But it's easy to remember." "That's the contradiction," Peyton said. "The easy one is the one that gets stolen first, and then everything opens at once. One leak and it's toxic, it spreads to every account like a spill." Maika looked at her password written on a sticky note under the keyboard and slowly peeled it off.

The two of them spent the last ten minutes building new passwords, long ones with numbers and capitals, and a system for remembering them that didn't involve paper. Maika typed her new fourteen-character password into the school portal, hit enter, and waited. The screen blinked, then welcomed her by name. "Twenty-six to the fourteenth," Maika said quietly, almost to herself. Peyton laughed and held up the paper covered in her scribbled math. "Don't even try to write that number down. It wouldn't fit."

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: William Strunk Jr.'s writing guide The Elements of Style, written in 1918, gives the rule 'Omit needless words.'
story:
Owen had written the same sentence three times, and every version still had the word "very" in it. Mr. Vu had distributed the drafts back at the start of writing club, and across the top of Owen's paper, in green pencil, stood one question: "What can go?"

"My whole story," Owen said, sliding the paper across the table to Kaius. "It's about the monsoon flood last summer. It's supposed to be exciting, but it reads like a report about weather."

Kaius read it slowly, tapping the desk. He stopped at the sentence "It was a very, very dark and stormy and rainy night." Then he pointed above his own desk, where a strip of tape held up a small card. Owen leaned over to read it. "Omit needless words," Kaius said. "It's from a writing guide by William Strunk Jr. The Elements of Style, written in 1918. My sister gave me the card."

"Needless like which ones?" Owen asked.

"Try one. Cross out something and see if the sentence still stands."

Owen copied his first paragraph onto the whiteboard and circled every adjective. Very dark. Very, very stormy. Big rain. Huge water. He erased "very" and "very, very," and the sentence stood. Then he erased "dark" and "stormy" and kept only "rain," because the rain already showed all of it. He stepped back and read the line out loud. "It was a night of rain." The room got quieter in his ears, the way a playground does at the first clap of thunder.

Next he counted his sentence lengths. Fifteen words, sixteen words, fourteen words, seventeen words. Every sentence the same size, like fence posts. He cut one down to three words: "Then it came." The paragraph suddenly had a rhythm, short and long, like footsteps hurrying and stopping.

Joanne walked past the board on her way to sharpen a pencil and read it over. "Better," she said. "What's the flood part? I want to feel it coming."

"Try this," Owen said, and wrote beneath the paragraph: "The water felt imminent that morning, the way a test feels when you haven't studied." Joanne laughed and gave him a thumbs-up, then went back to her seat.

At the end of club, Owen taped his own card above his desk, copying the words in careful pencil: Omit needless words. Under it he wrote one more line, small enough that only he would notice. "Then make the rest count." He slid his draft into his folder, first page on top, and carried it out into the hallway, where the windows had gone grey with evening rain.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: In the dark, the eyes slowly grow more sensitive as rod cells in the retina rebuild a light-sensitive pigment called rhodopsin, which takes half an hour or more.
story:
The lights at Grandpa's house died just as Sadie found the good hiding spot for their game of hide-and-seek, and now she stood in the hallway unable to see her own hand in front of her face. "Jordyn?" she whispered into the blackness. "Are you still there?"

"Right behind you," Jordyn's voice said, closer than expected. "I was going to find you in ten seconds, but now I can't find anything. I can't even find the wall."

Sadie reached out and patted the air until her fingers bumped a doorframe. "Grandpa!" she called toward the kitchen. "Is the whole street out?" Grandpa's voice floated back saying the neighbors' porch lights were dead too, and that the flashlight was probably in the junk drawer, if anyone could find the junk drawer. That was the problem, Sadie realized. They needed light to find the light.

Then she remembered a night two summers ago, during a blackout at this same house, when Grandpa had carried her out to the porch to look at stars. At first she had seen nothing but black, and she'd complained that the sky was empty, which Grandpa said was a naive thing to expect from a city sky. But by the time they'd finished arguing about whether hot dogs counted as sandwiches, the stars had come out in the hundreds. She hadn't imagined them. Her eyes had changed somehow.

"Grandpa," she called, "that night on the porch, why did the stars show up later? Not the clouds. Us." Grandpa shuffled toward her voice and said that in the dark the eyes slowly grow more sensitive as rod cells in the retina rebuild a light-sensitive pigment called rhodopsin, which takes half an hour or more. "So if we sit still and don't look at anything bright," Sadie said slowly, "we'll be able to see the furniture without a flashlight?" Grandpa said that was about the size of it, and Jordyn groaned that half an hour of sitting in the dark doing nothing sounded worse than homework.

"It's not nothing," Sadie said, dropping onto the couch and pulling Jordyn down beside her. "It's an experiment. We're testing a rule about our own eyeballs. That's more science than the whole curriculum at school." They sat in the dark, and she counted out the minutes in whispers, checking her hand every so often. At first it was a pale blob. Then the blob grew fingers. By the time she had counted past thirty minutes, she could see the coffee table, the shape of the armchair, even the junk drawer in the kitchen, gleaming faintly like a challenge.

"Salvage mission," Sadie announced, standing up. "Follow me, and try not to walk into the umbrella stand again."

"Once," Jordyn said. "I walked into it once."

Sadie was already crossing the kitchen, one sure step at a time, her hand landing on the drawer handle in the dark.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Aaron had only eleven followers, and his account was private, so he felt safe posting the photo of himself in the translucent rain poncho from the lost-and-found fashion show he and Jamie had invented at recess. The caption read "Runway king." By the next morning, three kids he did not even follow were snickering at it in the hallway, and one of them demonstrated the whole joke on his own screen, holding the picture up like evidence at a trial. "The jury finds the runway king guilty," the kid said, and his friends laughed.

Aaron cornered Jamie by the lockers. "You shared my post?" Jamie's face went pink. "No. I didn't. I only liked it." That afternoon a message appeared on Aaron's screen from Jamie: "I swear I didn't send it to anyone. Check who follows you. Not everyone who follows you is your friend." Aaron read it three times. He scrolled his follower list. There was Fynn, a boy from his old school who had followed him back in September after one soccer tryout. Aaron had accepted without thinking. They had never spoken since.

So private had not protected him, Aaron realized, because private only kept out people who were not followers. Anyone already let in could still copy what they saw and pass it on. He wanted proof, though, not a guess. He posted a new private photo of the empty gym with the words "Secret demo, lunch, gym, tell no one," and told no one anything. Then he ate his sandwich in the library and waited.

At 12:15 he walked past the gym on his way to the water fountain. Fynn was there, alone, peering through the gap in the door. Aaron stopped beside him. "You got my post." Fynn shrugged. "You posted it. I can show it to whoever I want." Aaron nodded slowly, took out his phone, and tapped the button that removed a follower, right there, where Fynn could watch him do it. "Not anymore," Aaron said.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
The bus smelled like rain and vinyl, and Alexa had her notebook open on her knees before it even pulled away from the school. She was trying to conserve space, filling every line, because the coach had posted the softball rankings that afternoon and her name sat near the bottom. "Batting average," Briar had said from the seat behind her, smug. "It's just math. You can't argue with math."

"Watch me," Alexa said. She turned around. "My uncle took me to a sports bar last weekend, and he told me about this book, Moneyball, by Michael Lewis, from 2003. It described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." Abygael, in the window seat, leaned over. "Meaning what?" "Meaning one number doesn't tell you everything," Alexa said. "A team with almost no money beat rich teams by looking at a different number. Our rankings are like a monarchy. Batting average sits on the throne and everybody bows to it."

Briar folded her arms. "So prove it." That was the problem, Alexa thought, watching the wet fields slide past the window. She couldn't see on-base percentage anywhere. It was hidden inside dozens of tiny moments, walks and hits and outs, all crushed into one ranking on a hallway wall. But she could dig it out. She flipped to a clean page and drew a grid. "You walk me through every time I've been up this season. Don't skip anything."

They worked through the whole twenty-minute ride. Abygael remembered the game against Lincoln, and Briar, reluctantly, recalled two walks and a hit batter that the batting average treated as nothing. Alexa tallied each one, her pencil moving faster as the numbers grew. By the time the bus hissed to a stop at her corner, the grid showed her getting on base more often than two girls ranked above her. "That's not sophisticated or anything," she said, showing Briar the page. "Just counting." Briar stared at it for a long moment, then pulled out her own pencil. "Fine. Do mine next."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Most food chains start with the sun, because plants and algae, the producers, use sunlight to make their own food by photosynthesis.
story:
Paisley spread her poster board across the kitchen table and stabbed her pencil at the blank page. Tomorrow she had to stand up in science class and draw a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator, then explain what happened if one link disappeared. Mr. Yilmaz had made it sound easy. It was not easy. Her first attempt had a frog eating a fly, and then a heron eating the frog, and it had come back with one red question in the margin: "Where does the frog's energy really start?"

"You're gnawing that pencil like it owes you money," said her older brother, dumping his soccer bag on the counter.

"It does owe me money." Paisley flipped the pencil around. She had called Johnny after dinner, and he had been no help at all. "He said start with the frog. Everyone starts with the frog, or the wolf, or the shark. But that can't be right, because then everything eats something that eats something and it never begins."

Her brother shrugged and went upstairs, because brothers were useless.

Paisley dropped her forehead onto the table. The poster smelled like glue and faintly like the pizza box it had been shipped under. Then she sat bolt upright. The frog. Where did a frog's energy come from? Flies. She drew the fly. And the fly came from... she stopped. Flies didn't eat rocks. Flies ate stuff that was alive, or had been. What was alive in a pond? Algae. Green scummy stuff. She wrote ALGAE in wobbly capital letters. And algae, she remembered suddenly from a page she'd half-read three nights ago, didn't eat anything at all. Algae were producers. They used sunlight to make their own food. That was photosynthesis, a word she now said out loud to the kitchen, twice, because it felt like a spell.

She drew the sun first, big and yellow in the corner, then the arrow down to the algae, then the fly, the frog, the heron at the top. Sun to scum to fly to frog to heron. It started with the sun. Most food chains started with the sun. She could hardly sit still.

Then came the test. Mr. Yilmaz would ask what happened if one link vanished, so she tried it, smudging out the fly with her thumb. The frog lost its lunch. The heron lost its lunch. The whole chain sagged. She wiped out the algae instead and the collapse got even worse, all the way down, because without the producers nothing above them could start at all. It was like pulling the bottom block out of a tower. She grinned so hard her cheeks hurt, which was when she anticipated the best part: she could show the class the erase test live.

At school, Johnny slid into the seat beside her, groaning. "I drew a shark first. Again. My poster looks like a restaurant menu with no kitchen."

Paisley held up her poster, sun blazing in the corner. "Start with this. Everything on your menu comes out of it."

Augustus leaned over from the other row, squinting at her arrows like an impartial judge. "So the shark's energy is really sunlight in a swimsuit?"

"Basically," said Paisley. "Wanna see it fall apart?"

She grabbed the eraser, aimed at the algae, and said, "Watch the whole thing go."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A cast saw's blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning, which lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath.
story:
Maria sat on the swings with her purple cast propped on her lap, doing nothing, because that was all the swings were good for now. Jaydon stood in front of her with the permission slip from the office flapping in his hand. "My mom signed it," he said, waving the paper. "Cast removal day. Yours is Thursday, right?"

"That's the suspense part," Maria said. "Waiting."

Jaydon's face went pale. "They use that saw. That ominous buzzing thing. I heard it from the hallway last time and it sounded like it was eating someone."

Maria had heard it too, three weeks ago, when she sat in the nurse's office waiting to get her own cast put on. A boy ahead of her had practically climbed the wall when the nurse approached with the saw. He'd been shrieking that it would cut him. Maria had watched closely, because she wanted to know if she should be shrieking too. The nurse had said, "It can't cut your skin," and turned it on, and held the spinning-nothing blade flat against the boy's own thumb. Nothing happened. Not a mark. Then she pressed it to the fiberglass and it chewed straight through like it was hungry.

Maria had spent the whole ride home thinking about that. A blade that cut hard cast but not skin had to be doing something different from a normal saw. She'd asked the nurse one question on the way out, and the answer clicked everything into place: the blade vibrated rapidly back and forth instead of spinning. That was the trick.

"It won't cut you," she told Jaydon now. "The blade vibrates back and forth really fast instead of spinning, so it cuts through hard plaster or fiberglass but it can't cut your skin."

Jaydon narrowed his eyes. "Then how are you getting out of the cast on Thursday, if it's so wonderful?"

"I'm not. I've decided to keep it forever and never use that arm again." Maria knocked on the cast with her good hand. "It's a great bracelet. One size fits me."

Jaydon laughed, then stopped. "Wait. Thursday. You're going first, before me? Good. If you scream, I'll know."

Maria stood up from the swing. "Deal. If I scream, you can have my lunch for a week."

She marched toward the doors, cast first, like a soldier.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: The law of supply says that when the price of something rises, sellers offer more of it, because producing it becomes more profitable.
story:
Mackenzie raced through the mall's east entrance with her notebook flapping, because today the strawberry price board at the fruit stand had finally changed, and she wanted to see it before anyone else did. Last summer she had copied the numbers into her notebook as part of her project for the school economics fair, where every seventh grader had to participate with a poster and a two-minute talk. In June, strawberries had cost three dollars a basket. In December, the same basket cost eight dollars, and she had stood there in her winter coat wondering why.

"They're still eight dollars," Aurora reported, holding up her phone so Leonie could see the photo she'd taken of the board. "Also, the smoothie place raised the berry blast by a dollar, which is a personal tragedy for me." Aurora's real mission today was the smoothie, and Mackenzie knew it.

"That's the thing," Mackenzie said. She flipped to her fresh page. "Watch. When the price goes up, watch what the sellers do." She counted the fruit stands along the market hall: one strawberry stand, the same one from December. She wrote "one stand, eight dollars" and drew a box around it.

"Why are you counting stands?" Leonie asked, peering over her shoulder. "That's a weird category of information."

"It's my test. I have this idea. I think when the price of something rises, sellers offer more of it, because producing it becomes more profitable. It's called the law of supply. So if strawberries stay expensive, more strawberry sellers should show up."

"That's a big if," Aurora said, but she skipped the smoothie line to help count anyway.

For two Saturdays they came back. The price held at eight dollars. On the third Saturday, Mackenzie walked in, stopped dead, and grabbed Leonie's sleeve. There were four strawberry stands in the market hall. Three new ones, stacked with baskets, all with handwritten signs competing for customers.

"Three," she whispered. "One turned into four."

Leonie pulled out her own phone and took a picture of the row of stands. "Your notebook is going to need another page."

Mackenzie sat down on the bench by the fountain and started a new chart, her pencil moving so fast it tore a little hole in the paper. "Ms. Whitaker is going to flip when she sees this."

Aurora returned balancing two smoothies. "I got you a berry blast. It cost me a dollar more, but I consider it a research expense."

"Put it here," Mackenzie said, patting the bench beside the notebook without looking up. "Right next to the numbers."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Practicing a speech out loud with a timer matters because reading silently is faster than speaking, so a speech often runs longer than expected.
story:
Sebastian had read his speech fourteen times without making a sound, and it seemed perfect. The topic was wind power, and he had a strong opening hook about standing under a giant turbine, three points about clean energy, and a closing that tied it all together. On paper, the whole thing felt like about a minute. The assignment from Mr. Sultani was two minutes, exactly, so Sebastian figured he had room to spare. He flopped onto the couch, read it once more with his eyes only, and felt ready.

His mother passed through the living room with a basket of laundry. "You're supposed to practice it out loud," she said. "That's what the sheet says."

"I did practice it," Sebastian said. "Twice." But when she was gone, he pulled out his phone, opened the timer, and stood up anyway. Maybe reading aloud would make it feel more real, like standing in front of the class. He set the phone on the coffee table and pressed start.

He began with the hook. "Imagine standing at the bottom of a wind turbine so tall that the clouds seem to lean on it." So far so good. Then his first point, about how wind farms could bring electricity to impoverished villages that had never had reliable power. Then his second point. He was partway through the third, the part about how the class could nominate clean energy projects for the school science fair, when he glanced at the timer and stopped cold. Two minutes had already gone, and he still had the whole closing left.

He sat down hard on the couch. Silent reading had lied to him. He grabbed a pencil and read aloud again, this time marking the paper wherever he could cut. He trimmed the story about the turbine repairman, tightened his second point, and crossed out an entire sentence about noise levels. When he ran it a third time, he finished with eleven seconds to spare, and he wrote a note at the top of the page in big letters: NEVER TRUST SILENT READING.

At dinner he told his father the whole thing, pencil marks and all. "Reading it in my head, it felt short," he said. "Out loud, it just kept going."

His father nodded. "So tomorrow, when you stand up in class?"

Sebastian pushed back from the table and headed for the stairs. "Timer's coming with me."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The cast shadow is the shadow the sphere throws onto the surface it rests on, and it always falls on the side opposite the light source.
story:
Cameron had decided his pencil sphere was actually a tiny planet, and the planet needed a sun. Ms. Kobayashi had set each of them a plastic ball on the table by the big window and told them to make it look round using only light and dark. Cameron squinted at his planet. Bright spot near the window, gray curve, and a dark rim on the far side. That much he could see. But when he tried the patch underneath the ball, his pencil hovered. Which way did it go?

Across the table, Emmeline was shading fast and confident, her pencil sweeping like a broom. Her ball looked ready to roll off the page. Then Dalie leaned over and laughed. "Emmeline, your shadow's on the wrong side. Look at the real one." Emmeline frowned at the table, where the actual ball's dark patch stretched away from the window, toward the room. Hers went toward the window instead.

"The cast shadow," Dalie said, pointing at the tabletop patch. "It's the shadow the ball throws onto the table."

Cameron felt like a scavenger who had just spotted a dropped coin. There was a rule hiding in the room, and Emmeline had found it the wrong way first. He devised a test, quiet and sneaky, the kind a planet explorer would run. He rolled his plastic ball slowly across the table and watched the dark patch travel with it, always stretching away from the window, always on the far side, as if it were frightened of the light. He tried a hypothetical version in his head: if the sun moved to the other side, the patch would flip. It was like the shadow was tied to the light by an invisible rope, always dragged to the opposite side.

He bent over his page and drew the patch on the side away from his pencil-sun, darkest where it touched the planet, fading out at the edge like a fading comet tail. Then he held the drawing up next to the real ball, one eye closed.

Emmeline came over and peered at his paper. "Yours looks real," she said. "Mine looks like it's floating."

"That's because your planet's shadow ran away from the sun," Cameron said, "and you chased it the wrong direction."

He turned back to his page and added one last line, a soft gray swoop, then set the pencil down on the table like a tiny spaceship landing.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
story:
The trouble started in the science chat on Tuesday night, while Leah was supposed to be labeling a diagram of a earthworm's intestine. She typed, "Our frog dissection is cancelled because the frogs unionized," and Khloe, who never joked back, replied with a long message asking which period it was cancelled for and whether they needed a permission slip for the make-up date. By morning, half the class believed it.

Mr. Ionescu had to clarify the assignment twice before homeroom, and he did it without ever looking at Leah, which somehow felt worse than being called out. At recess she sat on the wall beside Elena and stared at her phone. "I thought everyone would know it was a joke," she said.

"Online nobody can hear your voice," Elena said. "That's not new, though. Somebody solved it ages ago."

Leah searched the name Elena had mentioned, Scott Fahlman. He had proposed the emoticon, a colon, dash and parenthesis making a sideways smiling face, on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. She read it twice. Almost forty years before she was born, people typing at computers had run into exactly her problem, and some guy had fixed it with three punctuation marks.

"He made the smiley face for this," she said. "For me, basically."

"He didn't know about you," Elena said.

"Details." Leah opened the chat, found her frog message, and typed a reply to Khloe: "That was a joke, sorry! :) " She hesitated before sending it. The little face looked almost too simple, almost obsolete in a world of animated gifs, but maybe simple was the point. She pressed send anyway.

Khloe's answer came before the bell: "OH. Okay. Can I still label my intestine diagram wrong on purpose as a joke? :)"

"Only if you make it a really good joke," Leah typed back, and grinned at her screen all the way down the hall.

activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: It takes about 29.5 days for the Moon to go from one new moon to the next.
story:
Nathaniel dragged the floor lamp into the middle of the living room and set a gray kickball on the coffee table, which he had decided was Earth. Tomorrow he had to explain the Moon's phases in front of the whole class, and his first try yesterday had been a disaster. He had told Mr. Ricci that the Moon made its own light and shrunk like a cookie with bites taken out of it, and Simona had laughed so hard she knocked over her chair. His dad let him take over the room after dinner, on one condition: no demolishing the lamp.

He unplugged the shade so the bare bulb shone like a small sun, then carried an orange around the table in a slow circle. Half the orange always glowed on one side, half stayed dark. He stopped and squinted. The bright part turned, but the bulb never blinked. "The Moon doesn't shrink," he said out loud. "We just see different slices of the lit half."

On Thursday he performed it for Simona and Mohamed-Amine before class, orange in hand. "The Moon's always half lit, same as this orange. When it's between the lamp and Earth, the lit side faces away from us, so we see basically nothing." He walked the orange behind the table and held it up. "That's the new moon." Simona frowned. "Wait, you said it disappears?" "No, I was wrong," Nathaniel said. "It's there the whole time. We just can't see the lit part."

Mohamed-Amine raised his hand like they were already in class. "My grandfather marks the Moon on his kitchen calendar every month. I counted his marks once. It takes about 29.5 days for the Moon to go from one new moon to the next." Nathaniel wrote 29.5 on his palm in pen. "So if tonight is a new moon, the next one shows up almost a month later. That's the pattern I can prove with this."

In class, Mr. Ricci folded his arms and watched, impartial as a referee, while Nathaniel orbited the orange. "New moon, thin sliver, half, full, half again, thin sliver, back to new. About 29.5 days, one whole lap." Mr. Ricci nodded slowly. Simona raised her hand. "Can I do the orange?" Nathaniel handed it over. "Watch the lit side," he said. "It never goes out."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Muffin tops turn golden brown in the oven because sugars and proteins react in the heat, a process called the Maillard reaction.
story:
The zucchini at Mr. Marino's stall was the size of Sydney's forearm, and she picked it up like a trophy. "One of these is going into my muffins," she announced. "My grandma's recipe. I'm baking them alone, start to finish, even the oven part."

"You've never preheated an oven by yourself?" Veer asked, juggling three lemons.

"Last summer I tried to bake tropical mango muffins at my cousin's house. I set the oven, mixed the batter, and slid the pan in, but they came out pale and gummy. My cousin still calls me the Ghost Muffin Maker, like a scavenger that haunts failed bakeries." Sydney paid Mr. Marino, who winked and slipped an extra zucchini into her bag as if it were contraband.

Lili-Rose walked home with her, carrying the bag of walnuts they'd bought from another stall. "Maybe the oven was broken at your cousin's," Lili-Rose offered.

"Or maybe it wasn't hot enough when the pan went in," Sydney said slowly, working it through. "Grandma's recipe says to preheat first, and I remember I got impatient. I put the pan in before the little light stopped blinking. But here's the part I never figured out. The tops got a tiny bit golden, only the tops. The insides stayed pale. Why would heat brown the outside and not the inside?"

Veer shrugged. "Heat can't reach the inside?"

"Then why brown at all?" Sydney turned the question over all the way to her kitchen, where she laid out flour, sugar, eggs, and the recipe card she had begun to cherish like a family treasure, soft at the corners from Grandma's thumbprints. She set the oven dial, watched the light blink, and did not open the door. While she grated zucchini and folded batter, she thought about the outsides of things, bread crusts, toast, the seared edge of a burger, all brown on the surface, all pale underneath. Same pattern everywhere. Something about the heat touching the outside.

She slid the pan in and, twenty minutes later, pulled out muffins with tops the color of caramel. Veer leaned in for a sniff and got a flick of flour on his nose, which made Lili-Rose laugh so hard she had to sit down.

"Look at that," Sydney said, breaking one open. Pale and tender inside, golden on top. "I read the label on the flour bag yesterday. The sugars and proteins react in the heat, and that's what browns the tops. It's called the Maillard reaction."

"Sounds like a pirate name," Veer said through a mouthful of muffin.

"Captain Maillard of the Golden Tops." Sydney held one up to the window light, grinning. "Now every single one of them gets eaten, Veer. Not you, me, and not the dog."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce an irritating gas, which reaches the eyes and makes them water.
story:
Ryan stood in the produce section holding two onions like grenades, one in each hand. "Yellow for soup," he told Kaylie, who was tagging along because her mom sent her for milk and she'd rather debate vegetables than go home. "Dad's working late, Mom's got the twins, so dinner is me. Soup me." Kaylie sniffed a red onion and recoiled. "This one's revenge-flavored." At the next bin, Mr. Hu, who ran the register and apparently the whole store's opinions, glanced over. "Chill your onions before you cut them," he said. "Cuts down the tears." Ryan filed that away and carried the yellows to checkout.

Back home, the soup pot waited, the carrots were diced, and the onions sat on the counter like a dare. The first cut squeaked under the knife, and within seconds his eyes burned and water poured down his face. "Wow," said Kaylie, who had followed him home to watch the disaster. "You perceive your soup that strongly?" Ryan blinked floods onto the cutting board. "It's not feelings! Something's happening. Watch." He set a whole onion on the table and stared at it. Nothing. His eyes dried. He cut one slice, and the stinging came right back, worse the more he chopped, the misery perfectly proportional to the number of pieces on the board. "So it's the cutting," he said, dripping. "Breaking it open releases some gas, and the gas gets to my eyes. The whole onion just sits there being innocent."

He ran Mr. Hu's idea next: an onion from the fridge, plus swim goggles from the hall closet. He looked like a raccoon astronaut, but he diced the rest without a single tear, sniffling only from laughter at Kaylie's face.

At dinner, his mom took one spoonful and froze. "Ryan, honey, have you been crying?" The twins nodded solemnly, like witnesses. "Only chemically," he said, and lifted his goggles off the counter. "Safety first."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Like humans, guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so they must get it from their food every day.
story:
Alexander carried the cardboard box across the backyard like it was full of glass eggs. Inside, tucked in wood shavings, sat a brown guinea pig with one white ear, adopted that morning from the rescue table outside the pet store. His dad had said the pellets, the water bottle, and the cage were all ready in the garage, and Alexander had nodded, feeling the weight of his first real obligation settle on him. He set the box down in the grass so the animal could smell the warm evening air, and Lilyanna leaned over the edge, already suggesting names.

"Pepper," she said. "Look at his ear. I'm calling him Pepper whether you like it or not." Lilyanna had wanted a guinea pig for two years, and her whole reason for coming over was to hold one. She reached in, scooped him up, and then frowned. "He's really quiet. Don't they usually squeak?"

For the first two days Pepper did almost nothing but sit in the corner of his cage, fur dull, eyes half shut, ignoring even the pellets Lilyanna rattled at him. Alexander lay on the garage floor with his chin on his arms and wondered what he was missing. He had food. He had water. He had soft bedding and a hiding house that Lilyanna had decorated with a drawing of a carrot. So what was wrong? He checked the pellet bag and noticed something odd: the label bragged about vitamin C added, but the bag had been sitting in the garage since summer, months before Pepper existed. Maybe whatever was added could go stale, like bread left out too long. He couldn't see it or smell it, but the timeline fit.

He grabbed his mom's tablet and typed in the guinea pig's symptoms. There it was, plain on the screen: guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so they have to get it from their food every single day. He read it twice, then said it out loud to Lilyanna. "They can't make their own vitamin C. It has to come from their food every day." So stale pellets might not be enough, and Pepper hadn't eaten a single fresh thing since he'd arrived.

The next morning Alexander sliced a red bell pepper into strips, sweet and crisp, the kitchen smelling sharp and green, and offered one through the cage bars. Pepper's nose twitched. He took the strip in his teeth, and for the first time he made a sound, a loud, rusty wheek that made Lilyanna shriek with laughter. She fed him a second strip and let him rest against her sleeve, which, she admitted, was all she had really wanted all along.

By the weekend Pepper was racing laps around his cage, popcorning straight up into the air, and Alexander taped a chart inside the garage door: one pepper strip, every day, no exceptions. He even wrote a note to his dad about buying fresher pellets. Then he opened the cage and Pepper zoomed out onto the grass, wheeking at the top of his tiny lungs.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Scooping flour straight from the bag with a measuring cup packs it down and can add noticeably more flour than spooning it in and levelling it off.
story:
The ovens at Ms. Weber's café had to be preheated before anything else happened, which Eve had learned the hard way last Saturday when a tray of blueberry muffins went in cold and came out pale and sorry. Today she turned the dial first thing, then read the recipe twice, all the way through, because recipes were sneaky and liked to hide steps at the bottom. Ayat and Bowen had talked Ms. Weber into letting them help, since the café was closed for the morning and there was a school project due on Monday about doing something new from start to finish.

They were all making the same muffins from the same page. Bowen grabbed his measuring cup, shoved it straight into the flour bag, and dug out a heaping scoop. Ayat did it differently, spooning flour into her cup bit by bit and sweeping the extra off the top with a butter knife. Eve watched them both, then looked at her own cup, which was somewhere in between, a little mounded, a little not.

"Does it matter?" Bowen said. "A cup's a cup."

"I don't know," Eve said, but it bugged her. Two cups of the same thing should be the same, unless something was happening that they couldn't see. She had a thought and went to find the scale Ms. Weber used for coffee beans. "Scoop your way into this," she told Bowen, "and Ayat, do yours."

Bowen's cup weighed more. Not a huge amount, but enough that if every cup in the recipe weighed a bit extra, there would be a lot more flour in his bowl than the recipe asked for. Eve wrote both numbers on the back of a receipt so they wouldn't have to argue about it later. "You're packing it down when you dig," she said. "Spoon it in and level it, and you get what the recipe wants."

"That feels invasive," Bowen said, holding his scooped cup like evidence at a crime scene. "You weighed my flour."

"You made it suspicious."

They filled the tins, and Eve slid them into the hot oven and set the timer, which was the part she was most proud of remembering. While the muffins rose, Ms. Weber came through for coffee and asked how the project was going. "We're testing a theory," Ayat said. "Don't tell us yours."

"My theory involves you three washing these dishes," Ms. Weber said, and left with her mug.

The batches came out different. Eve's were good, and Ayat's were light and tall, but Bowen's, the ones from the packed cups, were squat and dry, dense as hockey pucks. He broke one in half, stared into it, and said, "It looked exactly like a cup of flour."

Eve slid the receipt with the two weights across the counter to him. "The scale says otherwise."

Bowen picked up his spoon, walked to the flour bag, and started over.

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
knowledge_domain: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
fact: Washing your hands before touching a cut helps keep germs from getting into the wound.
story:
Mila sat on the lobby bench at First Community Bank, waiting for her mother to finish her shift. She was rereading a text from Eloise, who had skipped the babysitting course they were both taking.

"I dropped out," the message said. "Too much stuff to memorize. Did you get to the part about cuts? What's the rule? I have to watch my little brother this weekend and he falls off things constantly."

Mila was typing a reply when the teller at window three swore and grabbed her thumb. He had sliced it open on the edge of a coin box. A thin line of blood welled up, and the manager hurried over, but the first aid kit under the counter only held bandaids and wipes.

"I can help," Mila said. "I'm taking a course." She had already noticed the drinking fountain and the small restroom beside it. "But first I have to wash my hands. Washing your hands before touching a cut helps keep germs from getting into the wound." She showed Eloise's text to no one in particular; it was the answer she had been about to send.

She scrubbed at the sink, dried her hands on a paper towel, and came back. The teller held his thumb over the wastebasket. Mila looked closely at the cut. It was shallow and the edges sat together, not gaping, so she tore open a bandage, wound it snug around his thumb, and pressed the ends flat.

"It doesn't need a doctor," she said. "But if it were deeper, or if the edges pulled apart, you'd want to get it looked at."

The teller flexed his thumb and picked up his carton of peach nectar with his other hand. "Diligent kid," he said. "Most people would've just grabbed it."

Mila finished her text: "The rule is wash first, then cover it. If it's deep or won't close, take him to a clinic." She hit send, and the manager handed her a lollipop from behind the counter.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
Rosalie had two tabs open on the family computer, and both of them claimed to be about the same thing. One headline said the school tax poll had risen 10 points, from 40 percent to 50 percent. The other headline, on a different site, called it a 25 percent jump. She leaned closer to the screen as if that would make the numbers agree.

"Those can't both be right," she said out loud. Her mother, folding laundry behind her, shrugged. "Maybe one site made a mistake." But Rosalie didn't think so. Mistakes were usually sloppy, and both of these stories looked careful, with charts and everything.

She texted Kierra, who was doing her own homework across town. Kierra wrote back in seconds: "r u sure it's the same poll?" Rosalie checked. Same pollster, same dates, the two articles had even used the same quote from the mayor. The numbers just refused to coincide.

Then Arthur chimed in from the group chat, because of course he did. "Ask Mr. Ferreira," he suggested. "He loves this stuff." But it was Saturday, and Rosalie didn't want to wait. She looked at the numbers again. Forty to fifty. Ten more out of a hundred. She typed 10 divided by 40 into the computer's calculator and stared at the answer: 0.25. Twenty-five. Both stories were true, she realized, sitting back so fast the chair squeaked. Ten points was how much it grew; twenty-five percent was how much it grew compared with where it started.

It reminded her of her grandfather, who had once given up a settlement from an old workplace dispute because a lawyer's percentage had sounded small to him and he hadn't checked. He'd regretted it for years, though he never said exactly how much money it had cost him. Maybe nothing, Rosalie thought, maybe a lot. She'd asked him once and he'd only smiled and changed the subject to the endangered cranes he liked to watch at the lake.

On Monday she cornered Mr. Ferreira by the gym doors. "Forty to fifty," she said. "Ten points and twenty-five percent, same change." He grinned and said, "Percentage points," and she said, "That's the phrase," and he laughed. "Most adults get that wrong in front of cameras." She walked to class composing a text to Kierra and decided she'd tell Arthur first. "You were right," she would type. "But I figured it out before he did."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death that usually includes a short account of their life, such as their family, work and interests.
story:
Justin found the folded newspaper page on his grandfather's kitchen table, wedged under a bowl of walnuts. At the top it said OBITUARY in bold letters, and beneath that, his grandfather's name, which made Justin's stomach drop even though he already knew, already stood in the emptied house while cousins and aunts moved boxes in the next room. He read the first line. Then he read it again.

"Grandpa was a sailor," he said out loud.

His cousin Dash leaned over his shoulder, chewing a walnut. "It's a published notice of somebody's death," Dash said, reading the header. "It usually has a short account of their life. Family, work, interests." He tapped the page. "Sailor. Two years on a cargo ship. He never told you that?"

"He never told me anything about ships." Justin turned the paper over, then back, as if more facts might germinate from the page itself. Grandpa had grown tomatoes, fixed lawnmowers, fallen asleep during westerns. Nothing about the sea.

Zakariya, who had come with his mom to drop off a casserole, wandered in and listened while Justin laid out his thinking. "If he was a sailor, there should be evidence," Justin said. "Sailors keep things. Knots, maps, something."

They searched the garage, the closet under the stairs, the high shelf in the bathroom where Grandpa kept his razor. Nothing. Justin sat on the basement steps, sure he was wrong. Maybe the obituary had made a mistake. Maybe his mom had sent in the details and mixed up a name.

But the obituary also said Grandpa had loved growing things from seed, and that part was so true it made Justin's throat hurt. So the sailor part was probably true too. He made a pivot in his plan and climbed to the attic he'd already checked once, this time pulling out the cedar chest he'd assumed was just blankets.

Inside, under a quilt, lay a brass compass and a photograph of a young man in a white uniform, standing on a deck with his arm around nobody, smiling like the whole ocean belonged to him. Justin held it up to the light.

"Grandpa," he said, "you could have told me."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Beans and peas host bacteria in small lumps on their roots, called nodules, that take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use.
story:
Jaxon knelt in the school garden with a ruler and a notebook, because on Friday the principal was going to judge the beds, and the class with the best harvest would win the golden trowel. His tomato plants were a problem. The two nearest the bean bed stood tall and green, but the three at the far end were pale and half their size. "Same dirt, same water," he muttered. "Same everything."

He thought about last summer, when his grandfather had pulled up a scraggly bean plant in the backyard and grumbled that it was good for nothing. Jaxon, watching, had noticed something odd that he still remembered: the roots had been covered with small lumps, like tiny beads on a string. Nobody had said what they were. Now he wondered if those bumps were the hidden difference between his tall tomatoes and his short ones, some invisible rule about which plants grew where.

Ayla and Ella arrived with the watering cans. Ella watered the beans and made a face. "Your bean patch is way too crowded, Jaxon. Ms. Asante said you have to thin them." So Jaxon excavated the smallest bean seedling, working the trowel deep so he wouldn't tear the roots, and lifted it out. Ella leaned close and shrieked. "Gross! Insect eggs! Burn it!" Ayla crouched down and looked carefully. "They're called nodules," she said. "My aunt grows beans. The bacteria in them take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use. Beans basically feed the dirt." Jaxon stared at the little beads and then at his pale tomatoes across the bed. "That's it. That's the rule."

He tested it. He planted a row of bean seeds in a circle around the sickliest tomato, patted the soil, and marked the spot with a popsicle stick. Then he recorded his guess in the notebook: beans near tomato, tomato gets better. Every day at recess he checked, and Ayla steered the wheelbarrow past him like a captain, calling one handle her rudder and shouting "hard to starboard" until Ms. Asante told her to walk the wheelbarrow, not sail it.

By Thursday afternoon, the test tomato had new dark leaves and had grown three centimeters. The pale ones further away had not. Jaxon dug gently at the circle of beans, found the roots already dotted with fresh nodules, and showed them to Ella, who said "okay, that's still gross, but useful-gross." On Friday the principal walked the rows with a clipboard. He stopped at Jaxon's bed, measured the test tomato, and looked twice at his notebook. "Beans feeding a tomato. Interesting plan." Jaxon crossed his fingers behind his back and whispered to the bean seeds, "Don't be vain on me now. Just keep it up till three o'clock."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: A persuasive essay's goal is to convince the reader to agree with a position or take an action, not just to give information about a topic.
story:
Jeremy spread his crumpled essay across the kitchen table and read the title out loud for the third time. "School Lunches at Maplewood Middle." His pencil tapped against a glass of cold water, leaving wet rings on the wood.

Kaaden leaned over from the other chair, chewing the last bite of his own sandwich. "Mine's about the plumbing in old houses," he said. "My dad says our pipes could freeze every winter because nobody regulates the temperature in the basement. My essay is six paragraphs of facts."

"Mr. MacLeod gave mine back with one word at the top," Jeremy said. "Not persuasive." He turned the paper over, hoping for more, but the back was blank except for a random doodle of a taco he had drawn during math. He had written everything he knew: the cafeteria served pizza on Fridays, the salad bar opened at noon, and the portions were small. None of it explained what he had done wrong.

Then Zac skidded into the kitchen, dropped his backpack on the floor, and grabbed the paper. "Wait, you wrote a report. That's just information about a topic." He jabbed the page with his finger. "A persuasive essay has to convince the reader to agree with a position or take an action. You have to want something."

Jeremy sat up so fast his chair squeaked. "So I pick what I want, then make them want it too." He yanked a fresh sheet toward him, and the smell of sharpened pencil filled the air as he scribbled fast. New title: Why Maplewood Needs a Second Salad Bar. Introduction, three reasons, conclusion, five paragraphs, exactly like the assignment sheet said. He wrote about the line that wrapped past the gym doors every day, the kids who gave up and bought chips, and how a second bar would cost less than the vending machine repairs.

"Read me the last line," Kaaden said, leaning in.

Jeremy held the paper up to the window light. "If you care what students eat, give them a real choice." He grinned and slapped the page flat on the table. "Mr. MacLeod is going to read this at lunch tomorrow."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Deodorants do not stop sweat; they fight odor by slowing the growth of skin bacteria and covering smells with fragrance.
story:
Evan sat in the waiting room with his arms clamped to his sides, because the gray patches on his blue shirt had come back by second period even though he had used Charley's deodorant that morning. He was here for his yearly checkup, but what he really wanted was an answer to a question he could not ask out loud. If the deodorant was working, why was his shirt still damp?

He remembered the day before, in gym class, when Nael had sniffed the air and said, "Okay, which one of us is that?" Nobody had answered. Evan had gone home and taken the longest shower of his life, and in the morning he had borrowed the deodorant from Charley's locker, hoping it would act like an umbrella for his armpits. It had not. He ran his thumb along the parallel stripes of damp on his shirt, one under each arm, exactly matching. Whatever was happening was happening on both sides at once, like a rule he could not see.

The nurse called him in, measured him, and said he'd grown two inches since last year. "That's puberty starting," she said. "Sweat glands wake up. Bodies change." She handed him a little booklet to look at while they waited. Evan flipped through it, past a page about vaccines and one about sleep, and stopped at a line that made him sit up straight. Deodorants do not stop sweat. They fight odor by slowing the growth of skin bacteria and covering smells with fragrance.

So that was it. He had the whole idea backwards. Sweat and smell were two separate problems, and the deodorant only worked on one of them, the bacteria one, the invisible one. When the doctor came in and asked if he had any questions, Evan said, "So deodorant can't keep my shirt dry? Nothing in it stops sweat?" The doctor shook his head, and Evan nodded slowly, deciding he would stop blaming the deodorant, and maybe stop borrowing Charley's too.

On the bus home he sat next to Nael, who was reading a comic. Evan peeled his shirt away from his side, felt the dampness, and let it be. "Guess what doesn't stop sweat," he said. Nael lowered the comic an inch. "What?" "Deodorant. It only fights the smell." Nael frowned. "Then what are you gonna do about the wet part?" Evan looked out the window and said, "Wear a darker shirt tomorrow."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The 'fundamental attribution error', named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, is the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in.
story:
Vincent stomped into the kitchen and dropped his sleeping bag on the floor like it had personally thwarted his entire weekend. "Maia didn't come to the sleepover," he told his mom. "She didn't even text. She's just selfish, that's all." He had planned the whole night, giant fort, three movies, a marshmallow tower contest, and Maia had said yes on Monday. Now the marshmallows sat in the pantry like evidence at a trial where the defendant hadn't bothered to show up.

On Sunday he decided to run a test. His hypothesis: Maia was a bad friend, one hundred percent character, zero percent excuse. To prove it, he would collect testimony. He texted their classmate Abbigail, who lived two houses from Maia. The reply came fast. "Didn't you hear? An ambulance came to Maia's house Friday night. Her grandma's really sick. Mr. Ramos told my dad they took her to the hospital downtown." Vincent stared at the screen so long his tablet went dark. His hypothesis crumbled like a marshmallow tower in rain.

He grabbed his mom's psychology book, the fat one she used for her night class, and flipped until he found it. "The fundamental attribution error," he read aloud to the dog, who seemed interested. "Named by a psychologist, Lee Ross, in 1977." The book said it was the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in. Vincent closed the book slowly. "Well," he told the dog, "that's me. Exhibit A: a total goofball."

He biked to the hospital with a get-well card and a bag of marshmallows, and found Maia in the lobby with her dad. Her grandma was sitting up and complaining loudly about hospital pudding, which everyone agreed was a good sign. Maia hugged him. "I thought you'd be mad." "I was," Vincent admitted. "Then I discovered I have a famous error named after people like me. Seventy-seven. That's the year, not my grade in science." Maia laughed so hard she snorted, and her grandma demanded to know who Lee Ross was. "Marshmallow tower rematch next Friday," Vincent said, holding up the bag, "and this time nobody gets sick."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, was the first U.S. state law requiring that a young athlete with a suspected concussion be removed from play until a health professional clears them.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and sweat, and forty kids were fighting for twelve spots on the travel team. Megan had practiced her crossover all winter for this. Two rows over, Muhammed ran the same drills, faster than almost everyone, which implied the coach was already watching him, and Megan needed to be just as impossible to ignore.

Halfway through the scrimmage, Muhammed went up for a rebound and came down wrong, cracking his temple against another kid's shoulder. He sat up slowly, blinking. The coach blew the whistle and jogged over, but Muhammed waved him off, called out that he was fine, and got to his feet. Everyone drifted back to position, and the whistle was about to blow again when Megan saw Muhamced's eyes. They tracked the ball a half second late, like a video buffering.

"Wait," she said, louder than she meant to. The whole gym turned. Her mouth went dry, because stopping a scrimmage could mean the coach remembered her as the girl who caused trouble instead of the girl with the quick hands. "He hit his head. That's a concussion, maybe. There's a rule about that." Mr. Warsame, the coach from the middle school who ran tryouts, folded his arms and asked what rule. Megan had done a history project on it last month, so she knew. "Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, the first state law in the country that says a young athlete with a suspected concussion has to be removed from play until a health professional clears them."

Mr. Warsame nodded once and pointed to the bench, and Muhammed argued the whole way there, saying he was fine, saying he'd lose his chance. Megan tried a hypothetical to test whether he really was fine: "If I toss you the ball, you'd catch it without moving your eyes?" He said sure, so she tossed it, gentle and easy, and the ball bounced off his forearm because he hadn't tracked it at all. He stared at his hands like they belonged to someone else. Somebody called his mother, and Muhammed walked out with a towel pressed to his head, promising the nurse would clear him by Thursday.

The scrimmage restarted without Megan for two minutes, and she spent them sure she had ruined everything. When the whistles finally ended, Mr. Warsame read the callback list, and her name was third from the top. He caught her eye across the gym and tapped the side of his own head, once, the exact spot where Muhammed's had bounced off the bone, not a fracture but close enough to matter. "First cut is Thursday," he said. "Tell your friend to bring his doctor's note."

activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
knowledge_domain: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
fact: A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel, one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking.
story:
Carson's grandfather had promised macaroni and cheese for dinner, but his wrist was sore from shoveling the walk, so the sauce was Carson's job. His cousins were arriving at six, and his grandfather had already boiled the noodles and shredded a mountain of cheddar. "The sauce is the whole game," his grandfather said from his chair by the window. "Lumpy sauce and it's a bowl of disappointment." He handed Carson a wooden spoon like it was the last piece in a game of monopoly, the one you refuse to trade no matter what.

Carson melted the butter in the pot, stirred in the flour, and watched it turn into a paste that smelled like warm toast. Then came the milk, and then came the lumps, small pale islands that no amount of stirring would dissolve. He tried to excavate one from the bottom of the pot with the spoon, but it only broke into smaller islands. His grandfather just said, "Try again," which felt tedious and unfair, because stirring flour and butter for five whole minutes was boring enough the first time.

While the second batch of butter and flour bubbled, Carson called Addison, whose dad cooked all the time. "Addison's dad makes this," she said over the phone. "He calls it béchamel. A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel, one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking." She said her dad heated the milk first, in a measuring cup in the microwave, and poured it in a thin stream while stirring the whole time. Carson stared at the smooth paste in his pot and thought about what was different. The lumps had to come from somewhere, and the only thing he had changed before was the milk, cold from the fridge and dumped in all at once. Maybe the hot flour grabbed the cold milk and clutched it into little balls. If the milk was warm already, and if he added it slowly, the flour would have time to let go.

He warmed the milk, set the pot over low heat, and poured a thin ribbon, stirring in slow circles, then faster, until the paste loosened into something glossy. The sauce thickened gradually, like paint, without a single lump. He drew the spoon through it and the trail stayed open for a moment before closing. Then he shut off the heat and folded in the cheddar a handful at a time until the whole pot turned smooth and golden.

At five fifty his grandfather limped in to check, dipped a corner of bread into the sauce, and held it up without a word. Carson tasted it too, sharp and creamy, better than the boxed kind. The doorbell rang, and somewhere down the hall his cousins were already arguing about who got the biggest bowl.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: A receipt lists every item and the amount paid, so reading it before leaving the till catches a scanning mistake while it is easy to fix.
story:
Jeremy's mother had decided that ten was old enough to retire the family rule about never crossing Maple Street alone. So on Saturday morning he stood in the grocery store with a five-dollar bill in his fist and one job: buy a carton of milk and bring back the change.

He found the milk, waited behind a woman with a mountain of coupons, and watched the cashier scan his carton. She handed him a receipt and two coins. Jeremy walked three steps toward the door, then stopped, because his mother had said one thing before he left: always read the receipt before you go. He had thought it was a silly instruction, like being told to look both ways on a sidewalk. He read it anyway.

The receipt listed every item and the amount paid. MILK 2.49. Then, below that, MILK 2.49 again. Two milks, but he was holding one. He counted the change in his palm, and it was short, almost exactly the price of a milk. He turned around and got back in line, feeling like a detective who had just solved a case nobody else knew existed.

"Excuse me," he said, laying the receipt on the counter. "It scanned my milk twice." The cashier frowned at the paper, tapped her screen, and said, "You're right, buddy. Good catch." She gave him another coin and printed a corrected receipt.

Walking home, Jeremy imagined telling Drayden and Gaelle about it. They had a running joke that Jeremy was the least sophisticated shopper in their class, the boy who once paid for a candy bar with a bag of pennies. But Drayden had once been plagued all afternoon by a missing two dollars at the arcade, and he never found out where it went. Jeremy now knew something Drayden didn't. He held the milk against his chest with one arm and read the receipt one more time on the corner of Maple Street, just to see his evidence, then folded it into his pocket and carried it all the way home.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: The muffin method mixes the dry ingredients in one bowl and the wet ingredients in another, then combines them only at the end.
story:
Bennett had never baked anything without his mom standing nearby, so when Jenny invited him over to make blueberry muffins, he decided he would do every step himself, start to finish. Jenny's kitchen smelled like cinnamon from the morning, and sunlight came through the window and hit the sugar jar, scattering little rainbows like a prism on the counter.

"First thing," Jenny said, tapping the recipe card, "preheat the oven to three seventy-five." Bennett turned the dial and watched the orange coils at the back of the oven begin to glow. "It'll emit heat for a few minutes before it's ready," Jenny said, sliding the muffin tin toward him. Bennett lined the tin with paper cups, then cracked the eggs into a big bowl, poured in the milk and oil, and dumped the flour, sugar, baking powder and salt right on top of everything.

"Wait, wait," Jenny said, picking up the card. "It says the muffin method mixes the dry ingredients in one bowl and the wet ingredients in another, then combines them only at the end." Bennett looked at his bowl, where egg was slowly soaking into a mound of flour, and groaned. "I just dumped everything in at once."

Jenny peered at the lumpy mess. "Can we save it?" Bennett thought about it. The wet stuff had only touched the top of the flour pile. He scooped the dry ingredients carefully off the top, spoon by spoon, into a second bowl, and when he reached soupy egg at the bottom, he figured he had most of it. Not perfect, but close. He whisked the wet bowl smooth, stirred the dry bowl, then folded them together until the batter just came together, flecked with blueberries. Jenny's little brother had a nut allergy, so she checked the ingredient labels twice before letting the batter near the oven, and Bennett read every one out loud for her.

While the muffins baked, a message popped up on Jenny's tablet from Bo: "Can smell something all the way from my house. Bring one to practice tomorrow or I'm quitting the team." Twenty minutes later, steam curled up from the muffin rack, and Bennett broke one in half to cool it faster. "The muffin method," he said, handing Jenny the bigger half. "You saw it here first."

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: Paid ads often appear at the very top of a search results page, above the unpaid results, so the first link is not necessarily the most useful one.
story:
The library computer hummed like a refrigerator with secrets, and Scarlett had exactly forty minutes before her mom picked her up. She typed "free math practice games" into the search box and pressed enter. The first result, shiny and blue, promised FREE for the first result on the page. She clicked it. The site loaded, asked for her grade, asked for her favorite animal, then asked for a credit card.

She stared at the screen. Credit card. She was eleven. Her wallet contained one dollar and a library card, and she cherished that library card more than most things she owned, but it would not unlock a math website.

"Stuck?" asked Domenic, sliding into the chair beside her with his own stack of books. He was supposed to be researching volcanoes but had instead spent ten minutes looking at pictures of the world's largest rubber duck.

"The top result isn't free," Scarlett said. "It says free everywhere, in like laser letters, and then it wants a credit card."

Domenic leaned over. "Click the second one."

She hesitated. It felt wrong, like reading the second question on a test first. Last summer, during the great lemonade disaster, she had trusted the first recipe she found, followed it exactly, and produced a liquid that Camryn had politely described as "angry." Camryn had spent that whole afternoon drinking it anyway, out of loyalty, and then texting Scarlett's mom a review that said never again. That was the day Scarlett had started to wonder whether the top of a list actually meant the best of a list.

She scrolled down and looked more carefully at the page. The first result had a tiny gray label next to it, small enough to miss, that said "Ad." The results below it did not have that label. So the first link had paid money to sit up there, above the unpaid results, which meant it was at the top because of money, not because it was good. The first link was not necessarily the most useful one. She tested the idea by searching something else, "free typing test," and sure enough, there was a labeled ad at the top of that page too, above the regular results.

"Ad," she said, pointing. "It bought its spot."

"So the internet is like a school fundraiser," Domenic said. "Whoever pays gets the front table."

"Basically." She clicked the second result, a plain, boring, impartial-looking site with no shiny buttons. It loaded instantly, asked for nothing but her name, and gave her twenty fraction problems. She got eighteen right.

"Rubber duck," Domenic said sadly, pulling his volcano books closer.

Scarlett grinned and typed "free volcano facts, no ads" into the search box for him. The second result looked perfect.

"Try that one," she said. "And check the label."

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Archaeologists found a workers' town and workers' tombs beside the Giza pyramids, evidence that the builders were organized, fed and honoured laborers rather than slaves.
story:
Leah clutched her museum worksheet at the edge of the war memorial park, where her class was waiting for the bus to the Egypt exhibit, and her stomach was doing flips.
