Tomorrow she had to present on why the ancient Egyptians built the pyramids, and right now all she had was one sparse paragraph about pharaohs and tombs. Bennett leaned against the memorial wall, grinning.

"Easy," he said. "Slaves built them. Whip cracks, chains, all of it. I saw the movie twice."

"That's the movie," said Manha, elbowing him. "Leah, ask the museum lady. Ms. Liu from the Egypt centre is meeting us there. She's my neighbour and she said we could look at anything."

Inside the exhibit, Leah drafted her plan on the back of her worksheet: first the pharaoh-as-god part, then farming on the Nile, then, if she could find proof, the builders. She stopped in front of a glass case and read the label twice. Archaeologists had found a workers' town beside the Giza pyramids, and workers' tombs beside it too. She turned so fast she nearly knocked over Manha.

"Bennett! Come see! There was a whole town right next to the pyramids, for the workers. And tombs for them. Right beside the pyramids, where honoured people got buried. You don't build a fancy tomb for a slave."

Bennett squinted at the display. "So they were... paid guys?"

"Organized, fed and honoured labourers, it says. Teams, probably, like a big project." Leah was practically bouncing. "And look, here's the Nile part. The flood made the fields rich, and the farmers had flood season off, so the work matched the farming year. The river shaped everything. That's my whole presentation, right there in two cases!"

Ms. Liu waved from across the hall, and Manha grabbed Leah's sleeve.

"Go tell her your theory," Manha said. "Test it on an adult before tomorrow."

Leah marched over, worksheet first, pen ready.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', economist Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price.
story:
The sign at the gas station read TWO BOTTLES PER CUSTOMER, and the cooler was almost empty. Ellie had walked three blocks in the heat for the last lemon iced tea on this side of town, and now Colton was reaching for the same shelf.

"Prices," Harlyn said from the door, holding up her phone. "Look, they doubled. It was two dollars yesterday."

"It's the store's fault," Colton said. "They just want more money."

"It's the buyers' fault," Harlyn argued back. "Everyone's buying it, so they can charge whatever."

Ellie stood between them, warm bottle in each hand, thinking. Everybody wanted iced tea today because of the heat wave, and there were only a few bottles left. She had read something in her brother's old economics book last week, something about scissors. "Neither one alone," she said slowly. "In his 1890 book, Principles of Economics, Alfred Marshall said it takes both blades of a pair of scissors. Supply and demand, both together, set the price."

Colton squinted at her. "Scissors?"

"Think about it. If the store had a hundred bottles, nobody would pay four dollars. If nobody wanted tea, they'd have to drop the price to sell any. It's both."

Ms. Petrov, their neighbour, was at the register with a frozen water bottle she would cherish on the long drive home. "You two can settle it," she said, nodding at the shelf. "There's exactly one bottle left behind the ice cream."

Ellie had an idea, and she wanted to test it right there. She checked the cooler again: one lonely bottle. Then she looked out the window at the road, where a line of cars waited for gas in the shimmering heat, every driver wanting something cold. Lots of buyers, few bottles, high price. It fit.

"I'll split mine," Ellie said, and grabbed two cups from the soda machine counter.

Outside, they divided the tea three ways under the awning, the air conditioning leaking through the propped door like the store couldn't quite hold its cool, the thermostat inside fighting a losing battle. Colton raised his cup.

"To the scissors," he said.

"Both blades," said Harlyn, and they clinked.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Repeating the same words at the start of several sentences is called anaphora; Martin Luther King Jr. repeated 'I have a dream' in his 1963 speech.
story:
Sofia stood at the kitchen counter with her note cards fanned out like a poker hand and groaned so loudly that her dad looked up from the dishes. "The speech is tomorrow," she said, "and my ending is worse than flat soda." Her problem was simple: the assignment from Ms. Ramos required a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and Sofia's three points about why the school needed a second recycling bin were fine. The closing, though, was one limp sentence that evaporated the moment she said it.

Ray came over after dinner, transporting a backpack full of snacks and his own note cards, because Ms. Ramos had assigned the speech to the whole class. He flopped onto the living room rug and made Sofia deliver her closing five times. "It just sort of dies," he said each time, waving a tortilla chip. "The ending needs teeth. Predatory, almost." Sofia laughed, but she knew what he meant; a good ending should grab you and not let go.

Then Ray sat up straight. "Wait. Remember the clip Ms. Ramos played, the speech from 1963? Martin Luther King Jr. said 'I have a dream' over and over, and it stuck in your head for days." Sofia grabbed her laptop and found the clip again. She listened to the crowd surge every single time the phrase came back, like waves hitting the same rock. She counted on her fingers. He started whole sentences with the same words, again and again.

"There's a name for that," Ray said. "I wrote it down because it sounded cool. Anaphora." He held up his card, and there it was in his messy handwriting.

Sofia tested it right there on the rug. Instead of her flat closing, she tried, "I want a school where nothing is wasted. I want a school where a bin is waiting where we need it. I want a school that proves we can do better." Ray's chip froze halfway to his mouth. "Okay, that actually gave me chills," he said.

They drilled until Sofia's little brother begged them to stop, and she made him listen too, timing her two minutes on the microwave clock. The next afternoon Ms. Ramos nodded along as Sofia hit her hook, ticked off her three points, and landed the closing. When Sofia said the last "I want a school" line, Ray, sitting in the second row, raised both fists silently, and Elissa mouthed, "chills."

The bell rang, and Ms. Ramos said, "Sofia, stay one second. That ending. Tell me where you found it."

activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: Plants store extra food as starch, while animals store it as glycogen.
story:
Alexandra crouched between the rows of potato plants at Ms. Sánchez's farm, a worksheet in one hand and a magnifying lens in the other. For her science class she had to draw a plant cell and an animal cell side by side, then label the parts only plants have, and she wanted a real plant to look at while she worked. The problem was that cells were too small to see, even with the lens, which felt like being handed a mystery with no clues.

"Those leaves don't imply much, do they?" said Philippe, kneeling beside her. He had come along because his mother ran the farm stand, and because Alexandra had promised him the last of her licorice.

"They imply plenty," Alexandra said. "Plants stand up straight without bones. Animals can't do that. Something inside the plant must be doing the job." She poked a leaf, watched it spring back, and wrote stiff wall? in the margin. Then she pulled a spade from the shed, chose a plant, and dug carefully around its roots until a cluster of potatoes came up trailing dirt. "And these," she said, holding one, "are the plant's lunchbox."

At the stand, Ms. Sánchez weighed the potatoes and laughed. "Full of starch, those. A potato is how the plant stores extra food." Alexandra wrote starch on her worksheet, then stopped. If plants stored extra food as starch, animals must store their extra food some other way, because she was pretty sure there was no starch sitting in her arm. She turned to Philippe.

"Where do you think my body keeps spare energy? I ate three pieces of licorice and I'm not using it all right now."

Philippe shrugged, so Alexandra made a plan to test it. She skipped lunch, waited until she was hungry and wobbly, then ran laps around the barn until her legs burned. When she stopped, doubled over, she still had energy to keep going if she had to. Something had been saved up and released, and it had not come from any potato. When she got home she looked it up in her science book and found the word glycogen, with a note saying animals store extra food as glycogen, not starch. She copied both words onto her worksheet in her neatest printing.

On Monday Ms. Sánchez visited the class to judge the cell drawings for a small scholarship prize, three books and a ribbon. Alexandra's poster showed a plant cell with its wall and green chloroplasts labeled, an animal cell beside it, and across the bottom, in molten-orange letters she had traced twice: starch in plants, glycogen in animals. Ms. Sánchez studied it a long time, then pinned the blue ribbon to the corner.

"That's the one," she said, and Alexandra grinned so hard her cheeks ached.

activity: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
knowledge_domain: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
fact: The Roman Empire reached its largest size around 117 CE, under Emperor Trajan, stretching from Britain in the northwest to Mesopotamia in the east.
story:
Jade spread the old atlas across Grandpa's kitchen table, weighting the curling pages with a teacup and a jar of nails. On Monday she had to stand up in front of her class and explain, using a map, why the Roman Empire split and fell, and right now she could not even find the borders. She had assumed the whole empire would be one tidy shape, like a puzzle piece. It was not. It sprawled.

"It's huge," said Rowan, who lived next door and had come over because Saturdays at Grandpa's were a ritual: cocoa, biscuits, and whatever project Jade was panicking about. Rowan ran a finger from the top of the page downward. "How far does it go?"

Grandpa shuffled over with his reading glasses and a battered encyclopedia. "There's a card in here somewhere," he said, flipping pages. Jade grabbed the book and found the entry herself, reading aloud. "The empire reached its largest size around 117 CE, under Emperor Trajan." She looked at the date under the map, then traced the border with her fingertip. It began in Britain, in the northwest corner of the empire, and went on and on, down past the sea and across to a land called Mesopotamia in the east. Her finger ached before she reached the end of it.

"That's it," she said slowly. "That's my whole explanation. Look how long this line is. Every bit of it needed soldiers, walls, watchtowers." She took the pencil and drew the border onto tracing paper, then held it stretched between her hands, thin and trembling, one end at Britain and one at Mesopotamia. "If you have to guard all of this at once, something has to give. It split because nobody could hold the whole thing."

Rowan leaned in and pressed one finger on Britain and one on Mesopotamia at the same time, arms stretched wide, like a bird trying to cover the atlas.

"That," Jade said, "is exactly my opening line."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: A fair coin toss gives each side an equal chance, which is why sports such as American football and cricket use a coin toss to decide how a game starts.
story:
The argument started before the bus even reached the corner. Eloi wanted the card game to begin with the red deck going first, and Everleigh insisted the blue deck had earned it because she had brought the cards in the first place. Their voices climbed over the rattle of the windows, and Rosalie, wedged in the seat behind them, could smell the pencil shavings Everleigh always kept in her jacket pocket.

"Blue goes first or we don't play," Everleigh said, arms folded.

"That's not fair," said Eloi. "You just dismiss every rule I make up."

"You're not making rules, you're making wins."

Rosalie remembered last summer, when she and her cousin had fought the same way over who batted first in the dusty lot behind her grandmother's farm. They had argued until the mosquitoes came out and ruined everything, and neither of them had gotten a real game at all. She had walked back through the agriculture fields that evening thinking she would rather lose a fair game than win a sulky one, though she had never managed to say it out loud.

She leaned over the seat now. "Can I try something?"

They both turned, suspicious.

"Name the problem first," she said. "The problem is nobody can tell who should go first, because both decks want it and there's no reason to pick one." She dug in her pocket and found a quarter, warm from her hand. "So we need a rule that isn't on anybody's side. A fair coin toss gives each side an equal chance." She showed them the two faces, one glittering, one ridged. "That's why big sports do it. In football, and in cricket too, they flip a coin to decide how the game starts. If it's fair enough for them, it should work for us."

"Cricket does that?" said Eloi.

"Cricket does everything," Everleigh said, but she sounded interested.

"Heads blue, tails red," Rosalie said, holding the coin above her knee. "First toss decides, and we toss again every new game so nobody gets stuck."

The coin spun, caught the morning light through the window, and landed. Tails.

Eloi grinned and began shuffling. "Every game?" he asked.

"Every game," Rosalie said, and dropped the quarter back into her pocket, where it settled with a small, definite click.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words, 'Veni, vidi, vici': I came, I saw, I conquered.
story:
Levi stood on Grandpa's porch steps, holding five index cards that trembled in the breeze coming off the garden. His speech on the space race was due Monday morning, and it was supposed to be two minutes long with an opening hook, three points, and a closing. He had seven points, and every time he practiced, he ran four minutes and forgot where he was.

"Grandpa," he called through the screen door, "how do I cut this down? My topic is about how satellites revolve around Earth, and the space race, and rockets, and dogs in space, and treaties, and all of it matters."

Grandpa came out with two glasses of lemonade and sat in the wicker chair. "You sound like my old commander. Everything mattered, so nothing did."

Levi frowned. He read the cards aloud again, and again he wandered. One card was about a treaty banning weapons in orbit, another about a stubborn Soviet engineer, and he couldn't drop either one.

"Did I ever tell you about Caesar?" Grandpa said. "Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words. Veni, vidi, vici."

"What's that mean?"

"I came, I saw, I conquered."

Levi stared at his cards. Three words. Three points. He laid the cards out on the porch boards and counted with his finger. "So if Caesar could win a battle with three, I can do a speech with three." He pulled out the rocket card, the satellite card, and the treaty card, and slid the rest under the lemonade glass. It felt like cheating, but when he timed himself on Grandpa's watch, he finished in one minute and fifty seconds, and he actually remembered point two after point one.

"See if it holds up in front of a real audience," Grandpa said, raising an eyebrow at the roses.

Levi turned to the flower bed and gave the whole speech to an obstinate bumblebee that refused to fly away, hook, three points, closing line and all.

"Ninety-eight seconds," Grandpa announced, tapping the watch. "You came, you saw, you conquered."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Many home ovens run hotter or cooler than the temperature on the dial, which an oven thermometer placed inside can reveal.
story:
The timer still had eight minutes left, but Ryder could already smell the edges turning dark. He pulled the muffin tin out, set it on the counter, and stared at six black-rimmed blueberry muffins, the third ruined batch since Saturday. His grandmother's recipe said twenty minutes at 375, and he had followed every line of it, including preheating the oven like the first step told him to.

"They can't all be for nothing," said Amari, who had come over to help carry the finished muffins to the team bake sale. The coach expected twelve edible muffins on the table at ten o'clock, and it was already eight. Ryder spooned batter into a new set of cups, but this time he didn't close the oven door right away. His dad kept a little dial thermometer on a hook in the garage, the kind with a metal probe, and Ryder fetched it and hung it from the rack inside.

"Genius or desperate?" Amari asked, watching him peer through the glass.

"Both," Ryder said.

The dial on the oven said 375. The thermometer inside read 415. Ryder leaned back on his heels. So the dial had been lying to him, and every batch had baked at a temperature the recipe never asked for. He turned the dial down to 340, and the thermometer crept back to 375 and stayed there. He hadn't been careless with the recipe; his oven simply ran hotter than the number on its dial, and now he knew it.

His mom came down in her robe, saw the thermometer glowing behind the glass, and smiled without saying a word, which Ryder took as a small victory. At nine-forty he pulled out twelve tall, golden muffins, and Amari fanned them with a cookie sheet to cool faster. Ryder set two aside on a plate for his mom, because she had a long shift ahead of her and never stopped for breakfast.

"You had a motive, didn't you," Amari said, nodding at the plate.

"Some things thrive on bribery," Ryder said, and closed the muffin tin with a clang.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Smokey Bear's campfire rule is drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat, because if a campfire is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave.
story:
On her second night at camp, Rose sat in the dining hall pushing rice around her plate while her cabin mates argued about the campfire ceremony. Salome wanted their cabin to earn the marshmallow roast on Friday, which meant passing the fire safety check on Thursday. "It's easy," Lucian said. "You dump water on it and walk away. Done." Rose wasn't so sure. She had watched the counselor at last night's fire pour water on it, then stir the ashes with a stick, then pour more water, and then crouch down and hold the back of her hand close to the coals. There had to be a reason for all of that, and Rose wanted to know what it was before Thursday.

At breakfast she found Mr. MacLeod, the counselor who ran the fire pit, and asked him straight out. "It's Smokey Bear's campfire rule," he said. "Drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat. If a fire is too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave." He emphasized the word "feel" by holding up his own hand. "You can't trust your eyes. Ashes can look dead and still be alive underneath." Rose turned that over all day. A fire could hide. It could look out and not be out.

On Thursday evening, her cabin built its fire, roasted one practice marshmallow each, and then Lucian grabbed the water bucket and dumped the whole thing on at once. Steam billowed up. "See?" he said. "Out." Rose shook her head. "You have to stir first, or the water just runs off the top." Lucian rolled his eyes, but Salome handed him a stick, and he stirred the black mess until chunks of glowing red rolled up from the bottom. Rose poured the second bucket over them, and they all watched the last ember hiss gray.

Then it was time to feel. Rose knelt and held the back of her hand above the wet ashes, the way the counselor had done. Warm. Not safe. "More water," she said, and Lucian, who had changed his mind about the whole procedure, was already sprinting to the spigot. When he came back and they stirred and poured again, Rose held her hand over the pit a second time. Cold as the gravel around it. "Okay," Lucian said, dropping the stick. "Now it's out." Mr. MacLeod walked over, checked it himself, and said, "Congratulations, girls. Friday, you roast." On the walk back through the dark, Salome said Rose was like an emperor of campfires now, and the title felt almost permanent, at least until breakfast.

fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:04, right after dinner. Ella typed first: "My mom said I can have the party. Now I just have to invite the whole class." Leon replied with three party hats and a question mark. Gurshan wrote, "Just put everyone's email in one big email, easy." Ella stared at her screen. Easy was exactly what worried her. Last year a boy in her class had sent a message to twenty people, and every single address showed up at the top, so everyone could see them all, and one kid got messages from strangers for weeks afterward. She typed, "I don't want to share everybody's addresses with everybody."

Gurshan, who was something of a chronic complainer, said that was overly complicated and that nobody cared anyway. Leon disagreed. "I care. My cousin had her address forwarded around once and it was a mess." Ms. Jean-Louis was in the chat too, because she ran the fifth-grade fundraiser and used the group to post updates about the revenue from the bake sale, which had reached eighty dollars. Ella messaged her directly: "Is there a way to email a lot of people without them seeing each other's addresses? I promise I looked before asking."

Ms. Jean-Louis sent back four words. "Look up BCC."

Ella did not ask her what it meant. She opened her email program and found a small link that said Add BCC, sitting quietly under the To line. She clicked it, and a new empty box appeared. She typed her own address into To, all twenty-four classmates into BCC, added the party details, and then, before sending it to everyone, she tested her idea. She sent the exact same message to just Leon and Gurshan, with her own address in To and theirs in BCC. If it worked the way she hoped, she would see proof.

Leon answered in seconds. "I got it. Weird thing though. It only shows your address. Like you emailed me alone." Gurshan wrote, "Same for me. Where's Leon's address?" Leon replied, "Nowhere. She used BCC. It means blind carbon copy. People in that field get the message, but the other people getting it can't see their addresses at all." Ella read the line twice, grinning so wide her cheeks hurt. Her test had worked. Hidden addresses, hidden from everyone but the sender, exactly as she had guessed.

Then she sent the real invitation, To herself, BCC the whole class. Replies poured in all evening, each one arriving as if Ella had written to that person alone. Gurshan sent a single message: "Okay, fine, you were right. Teach me how to do that." Ella typed back, "Saturday, at the party. Bring snacks."
